# UHECR energy threshold in the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review

## 0. Answer

**Threshold: 1 EeV = 10^18 eV** (per-particle total energy).
**Boundary: exclusive** — the review defines UHECRs as cosmic rays with energy *in excess of* 1 EeV, i.e. **E > 1 EeV**. The value 1 EeV itself is not included by the wording.

## 1. Source record (what was read, and how to check it)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Document | *Review of Particle Physics*, 2024 edition — Sec. 30, "Cosmic Rays" |
| Authorship line | Written October 2023 by J. Alvarez-Muñiz (Santiago de Compostela U.), Z. Cao (IHEP Beijing), U.F. Katz (Erlangen U.), P. Mertsch (TTK, RWTH), C. Spiering (DESY, Zeuthen) |
| Publication | S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024) |
| File read | https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf |
| PDF build stamp | "19th September, 2024" |
| Fetch sha256 (harness) | c8f0620d58d3… |
| Edition note | 2024 Highlights: "Major revision of Cosmic rays review, now covering all components of cosmic rays including neutrinos" — so the 2024 chapter, not an earlier one, is the correct target |

Reproduction: open the URL above, search the text for the string `ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)`; it occurs once, in the introductory paragraphs of Sec. 30.1, immediately after the galactic/extragalactic-origin discussion that accompanies Fig. 30.2.

## 2. The defining passage (verbatim)

> "…Direct and indirect observations therefore also largely refer to galactic/extra-galactic sources, respectively. **CRs with energies in excess of 1EeV are referred to as ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs).**"

Preceding sentence, for context (same paragraph): "Between hundreds of MeV and at least a few PeV, CRs are believed to be of galactic origin; above a few EeV, the sources are most likely extra-galactic."

This is the only sentence in the 2024 chapter that *defines* the term UHECR; every other occurrence of "UHECR" in the chapter uses the term without redefining it.

## 3. Why the boundary is exclusive

The operative phrase is **"in excess of 1EeV"**. "In excess of X" denotes strictly greater than X; a cosmic ray of exactly 1.000 EeV is not "in excess of" 1 EeV. The review uses this construction deliberately and contrasts it elsewhere with explicitly inclusive or explicitly bounded forms:

- Same chapter, §30.4 (anisotropy): "a large-scale dipolar anisotropy at **energies above 8EeV**" — again strict.
- Same edition, Sec. 36 (different chapter): "an extensive air shower (EAS) is produced by the interactions of **ultra high-energy (E > 10^17 eV)** subatomic particles" — the review's authors write the inequality out in symbols when they intend a formal cut; the Sec. 30 UHECR sentence is the prose equivalent, with the same strict sense.

No passage in the 2024 cosmic-ray chapter writes "≥ 1 EeV", "1 EeV and above", or "at least 1 EeV" for UHECRs. **Verdict: exclusive (E > 1 EeV).** If a downstream user needs an inclusive convention, that is a change of definition, not a reading of the PDG.

## 4. Units, convention, uncertainty, sample size

- **Unit conversion:** 1 EeV = 10^18 eV = 1 ZeV (the chapter's opening line uses "close to 1 ZeV" as the top of the charged-CR range, consistent with 1 EeV = 10^18 eV).
- **Energy convention:** per-particle **total** energy E, the same variable in which the review plots the all-particle spectrum (Fig. 30.1, abscissa E). The review does use per-nucleon energy where it means to — Fig. 30.2 is labelled "Cosmic ray flux at Ek/n = 20 GeV/n" — so the unqualified "energies" in the UHECR sentence is total energy, not energy per nucleon. (Inference from the chapter's own usage; the sentence itself does not spell out "total".)
- **Uncertainty:** none is quoted. The statement is **definitional, not a measurement** — there is no central value ± error, and no confidence interval. It is a naming convention (the review's own framing: CRs "are referred to as" UHECRs).
- **Sample size:** not applicable — no events, no dataset, no fit underlie this sentence. N = 0 measurements enter it.
- **Physical sharpness:** the threshold is conventional, not a spectral feature. The chapter's physically motivated landmarks are the knee (a few PeV), second knee (~100 PeV) and ankle (a few EeV), all stated with "a few" / "∼". The 1 EeV UHECR line is stated without "∼" precisely because it is a bookkeeping boundary, and the review's own text places the galactic→extragalactic transition at "a few EeV", i.e. near but not identical to 1 EeV. A user should not treat 1 EeV as an edge in the data.

## 5. Disambiguation: other 2024-PDG numbers that are NOT the UHECR threshold

Listed so that no value in this deliverable is read as competing with the 1 EeV answer.

| Number | Where (2024 edition) | What it actually is | Relation to the answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1 EeV (10^18 eV)** | Sec. 30, Cosmic Rays, §30.1 | **The UHECR definition** | **This is the answer** |
| 10^17 eV (E >) | Sec. 36, Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics, §36.2.1 (Wiencke, rev. March 2024) | Energy above which an air shower is called "ultra high-energy" for fluorescence-detector purposes | Detector-chapter usage, a decade lower; does **not** override the cosmic-ray review's definition |
| 5 × 10^19 eV (E >) | Sec. 36, cosmogenic-neutrino paragraph | Threshold for UHE protons photo-pion-producing on the CMB (Δ+ resonance) | Interaction threshold, not a UHECR definition |
| 8 EeV | Sec. 30, §30.4 | Energy above which Auger's dipole is measured (6.9σ) | Analysis threshold |
| 38 EeV | Sec. 30 (CenA excess; starburst correlation) | Anisotropy analysis cut | Analysis threshold |
| 57 EeV | Sec. 30 (Telescope Array hot spot) | Anisotropy analysis cut | Analysis threshold |
| "a few EeV" | Sec. 30, §30.1 and ankle discussion | Galactic→extragalactic transition / ankle | Qualitative, not the definition |
| "∼50 EeV" | Sec. 30, cutoff discussion | Flux suppression / E_max | Spectral feature |

If the request had meant Sec. 36 rather than Sec. 30, the answer would be E > 10^17 eV (exclusive). It does not: the request says "cosmic-ray review", which is Sec. 30, and that chapter carries the explicit definition.

## 6. Cross-edition stability check

The 2023 edition (https://pdg.lbl.gov/2023/reviews/rpp2023-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf, build stamp "1st December, 2023", sha256 5921cc31d87c…) contains the identical sentence: "CRs with energies in excess of 1EeV are referred to as ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)." The 2024 chapter is a major revision (neutrinos folded in) yet the definition is carried over word for word. This raises confidence that 1 EeV / exclusive is the intended PDG position and not a one-edition drafting slip.

## 7. What would change this answer

- If a 2024 PDG passage elsewhere stated "≥ 1 EeV" or "1 EeV and above" for UHECRs — none was found in the chapter; the verdict would flip to inclusive.
- If the requester intended Sec. 36 (non-accelerator detectors) — the value would become 10^17 eV, still exclusive.
- If the requester intended the Auger/TA community convention of 10^19 eV — that convention is *not* what the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review states, and adopting it would misreport the source.

*Draft for review by a qualified scientist before citation or publication. All quotations are verbatim from the cited PDF build; the sha256 prefixes are those recorded at fetch time and should be re-verified against the live file before this is used in print.*

# Equatorial-minus-polar radius difference of the Earth

DRAFT — arithmetic and sourcing for review by a qualified scientist before citation or publication.

## 1. Question and scope

Compute the difference (equatorial radius) − (polar radius) for Earth, in kilometres, from the two values given in the request as taken from NASA's Earth Fact Sheet.

Deliverable type: deterministic arithmetic on two published constants. No sampling, no measurement, no statistical test.

## 2. Source and input values

Source cited: NASA Earth Fact Sheet, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), Goddard Space Flight Center (fact-sheet entry for Earth). The two values below are used exactly as supplied in the request:

| Quantity | Symbol | Value | Unit | Digits after decimal | Implied resolution |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equatorial radius | a | 6378.137 | km | 3 | 0.001 km (1 m) |
| Polar radius | b | 6356.752 | km | 3 | 0.001 km (1 m) |

n = 2 input values (both published constants; no sample). The Fact Sheet is revised periodically — the reviewer should pin the access date / revision of the page when the figure is cited; this does not affect the arithmetic, which uses the two numbers as stated in the request.

## 3. Sign convention

The subtraction is defined as equatorial minus polar, in that order:

  Δr = a − b

Because a > b, Δr is positive. The ordering is fixed here so the sign cannot be misread downstream.

## 4. Computation

Step 1 — align by place value and subtract (km):

      6378.137
    − 6356.752
    ----------
         21.385

Step 2 — independent check by addition:

  6356.752 + 21.385 = 6378.137  ✓ (recovers a exactly)

Step 3 — unit restatement (no change of value):

  Δr = 21.385 km = 21 385 m

**Result: Δr = a − b = 21.385 km.**

## 5. Uncertainty

Inputs are quoted to the nearest 0.001 km (1 m). A difference preserves absolute resolution, so the result is meaningful to 0.001 km.

- Worst-case rounding bound (each input independently off by up to ±0.0005 km): ±(0.0005 + 0.0005) = ±0.001 km.
- Treated as independent rectangular rounding errors combined in quadrature: √(0.0005² + 0.0005²) = 0.0007 km (k = 1).

Reported: **Δr = 21.385 km ± 0.001 km** (rounding-only bound, conservative). No physical/geodetic uncertainty is propagated because the Fact Sheet values are quoted constants of a reference ellipsoid, not independent measurements; this is an assumption, stated explicitly.

## 6. Rounding and significant-figure policy

The result is reported at the full precision implied by the inputs (three decimals in km, i.e. 1 m). No further rounding is applied. If a coarser figure is needed, 21.39 km (2 d.p.) and 21.4 km (1 d.p.) are the correctly rounded alternatives; the headline value remains 21.385 km.

## 7. Cross-check against the defining ellipsoid (robustness, not a substitute for the answer)

The two quoted values are the WGS84 defining ellipsoid constants rounded to the metre:

- a = 6 378 137.0 m (exact by definition)
- 1/f = 298.257223563 (exact by definition) ⇒ b = a(1 − f) = 6 356 752.3142 m
- Exact difference: a − b = 21 384.6858 m = 21.384686 km → rounds to **21.385 km** at the stated 0.001 km precision.

So the quoted pair and the defining ellipsoid agree at the precision reported, and the exact WGS84 difference (21.3847 km) lies inside the stated ±0.001 km bound around 21.385 km. No inconsistency with the reported value.

## 8. Secondary context (not the requested answer)

| 6378.137 | quoted, NASA Earth Fact Sheet (as given in request) | km | ±0.0005 (rounding) | 1 |

| 298.25 | 1 / 0.0033529 | dimensionless | ≈ ±0.02 | 2 inputs |

# Sutherland constant S for U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 (NTRS 19770009539): corrected value and magnitude of the document's error

Draft for review by a qualified scientist before the code change is committed or any result computed with it is published.

## 1. Answers

| Ask | Answer | Unit | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|

## 2. Source trail (traceable to the cited documents)

**Errata (the authority named in the request).** Appended to the NTRS distribution file `https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19770009539/downloads/19770009539.pdf`, under the heading "Errata Sheet for 19770009539.pdf, U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976", item (2) of the enumerated list of errors in Table 2, B. Category II Constants, page 2, reads verbatim:

> "2) The value for Sutherland's constant S is too small by 0.4. It should be 110.4 Kelvin."

**Original document value.** The same report, body text on the defining constants (DTIC scan ADA035728, `https://archive.org/stream/DTIC_ADA035728/DTIC_ADA035728_djvu.txt`), reads verbatim:

> "The Sutherland constant, S = 110 K, (Hilsenrath et al. 1955) is a constant in the empirical expression for dynamic viscosity."

**Arithmetic.** 110.4 K − 110 K = 0.4 K. The errata's stated difference and its stated corrected value are mutually consistent; there is no rounding ambiguity at the 0.1 K resolution at which the constants are printed.

**Provenance, disclosed.** The errata sheet in the NTRS file is a forwarded email dated 8 January 2015 from Yekta Gursel to the NASA STI Information Desk, i.e. a reader-submitted correction archived with the distribution file, not a separately issued NASA revision. Its item (1) (r0 "too large by a factor of 1,000 in km") appears to be a units-header misreading, since the report's body text gives r0 = 6356.766 km, the correct value. This does not undermine item (2), which is independently corroborated in §3 below. A reviewer should nonetheless record that the S correction rests on (a) the errata text and (b) the internal consistency check, not on a formal NASA change notice.

## 3. Independent verification against the document's own tables

The report's viscosity law is the two-parameter Sutherland form

    mu(T) = beta * T^(3/2) / (T + S)

with beta = 1.458e-6 kg / (s * m * K^0.5) and S in kelvin (both constants attributed to Hilsenrath et al. 1955 in the report). Evaluating at the standard sea-level temperature T = 288.15 K (the report's T0, itself a defined constant, exact by definition):

- S = 110.0 K: mu = 1.458e-6 × 4891.34 / 398.15 = **1.79118e-5 Pa·s**
- S = 110.4 K: mu = 1.458e-6 × 4891.34 / 398.55 = **1.78938e-5 Pa·s**

The value tabulated in U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 at sea level is 1.7894e-5 kg/(m·s). Only S = 110.4 K reproduces it (agreement to all five printed significant figures). Conclusion: the tables were computed with S = 110.4 K; the "110 K" in Table 2 is the typographical entry the errata identifies. This check is a deterministic hand calculation (n = 1 per temperature, no sampling); its only uncertainty is last-digit rounding of the intermediate T^(3/2) = 4891.34 (five significant figures), which is below the 1e-9 Pa·s level and cannot move the conclusion.

## 4. Downstream impact of the correction (for the reviewer's sign-off)

All entries computed by me from mu = 1.458e-6·T^(3/2)/(T+S), T in K, mu in Pa·s (= kg·m^-1·s^-1), five significant figures, single deterministic evaluation per row:

| T (K) | mu, S = 110.0 K (Pa·s) | mu, S = 110.4 K (Pa·s) | Excess of uncorrected code |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 6.9429e-6 | 6.9297e-6 | +0.190 % |
| 200 | 1.33027e-5 | 1.32856e-5 | +0.129 % |
| 288.15 | 1.79118e-5 | 1.78938e-5 | +0.101 % |
| 1000 | 4.15370e-5 | 4.15220e-5 | +0.036 % |

Excess computed exactly as (T + 110.4)/(T + 110.0) − 1, which decreases monotonically with T as the table shows. Practical consequence: the uncorrected code over-predicts dynamic viscosity by at most ~0.2 % (coldest temperatures) and ~0.1 % at sea level; kinematic viscosity and Reynolds number inherit the same relative error with opposite sign (Re low by ~0.1 % at 288.15 K). This is below the 0.4 K correction's face value of 0.36 % of S itself — the two percentages are different quantities and must not be conflated in the write-up. If the model's validation tolerance is tighter than 0.1 % on Re or on viscosity-driven quantities, the correction is material; otherwise it is a documentation fix.

## 5. Change to make in the code

Replace the constant only; no other parameter needs to change, because beta = 1.458e-6 kg/(s·m·K^0.5), T0 = 288.15 K and the functional form are unaffected by this errata item.

- Before: `S = 110` (K) — e.g. Fortran `REAL,PARAMETER:: SUTH = 110.0`
- After: `S = 110.4` (K) — e.g. Fortran `REAL,PARAMETER:: SUTH = 110.4  ! Sutherland's constant, K`
- Units: kelvin. T must also be supplied in kelvin. Do not enter −162.75 (the Celsius equivalent) or 110 (the uncorrected value).
- Precision: carry 110.4 as printed (four significant figures, 0.1 K resolution). Do not round to 110 or to 110.40 in a single-precision literal that could re-round; a default REAL (or float64) literal 110.4 is sufficient and introduces < 1e-6 K representation error.
- If the code instead uses the reference-point form mu = mu_ref·(T/T_ref)^(3/2)·(T_ref + S)/(T + S), the same S = 110.4 K applies unchanged; mu_ref and T_ref must be mutually consistent with S = 110.4 K (e.g. mu_ref = 1.7894e-5 Pa·s at T_ref = 288.15 K), otherwise the two-parameter and reference-point forms will disagree.

## 6. Falsifiers — what would overturn these answers

1. If page 2, Table 2, B. Category II of the PDF actually prints S = 110.4 K, the errata's premise fails and ask 3 has no answer. (Checked indirectly: the body text and the errata both point to 110 K in the table; a direct read of page 2 of the PDF by the reviewer is the decisive check.)
2. If the sea-level tabulated viscosity in the report were 1.7912e-5 rather than 1.7894e-5 kg/(m·s), the tables would have been computed with S = 110 K and the errata would be wrong. My computation says they were not.
3. If the errata's "0.4" were a relative figure (0.4 %), the corrected value would be 110.44 K, not 110.4 K. The errata's own next sentence ("It should be 110.4 Kelvin") fixes it as an absolute 0.4 K.
4. If the code's S is used in a Celsius-referenced Sutherland form (some legacy formulations use S referenced to 0 °C), a direct 110.4 K substitution would be a units error. The reviewer must confirm the code's formula divides (T + S) with T in kelvin.

## 7. Adjacent errata items the reviewer should check but which are outside this request

- Page 2, Table 2, A. Category I: the errata reports R* differing by a factor of 10^6 from the value on page 3, paragraph 1, and states the page-3 value is correct. If the code reads R* from Table 2, that is a separate, much larger defect.
- Page 19, eq. (53) vs Table III (pages 98–114): the errata reports the tabulated thermal-conductivity column as too small by a factor of 1000. The errata's own worked check at 0 m, 288.15 K (eq. 53 gives 2.5326e-2 J/(m·s·K); Table III gives 2.5362e-5) is arithmetically coherent. Only relevant if the code consumes the thermal-conductivity tables rather than eq. (53).
- Errata item (1) on r0 appears to be a misreading (see §2) and should not be acted on.

## 8. What the reviewer must do before this is run or published

1. Open page 2 of the PDF and confirm Table 2, B prints S = 110 K (falsifier 1).
2. Confirm the code's viscosity routine uses T in kelvin and the (T + S) denominator (falsifier 4).

DOCUMENTARY DETERMINATION — DRAFT FOR REVIEW. This is a reading of a stated validity region, not a measurement or a re-derivation. There is no experimental sample; sample size for the claim is N = 1 primary document, checked in two independently fetched copies (§6). Units are stated at every number; βγ is dimensionless throughout (βγ ≡ p/Mc).

===========================================================
1. THE GOVERNING SENTENCE, VERBATIM, AND ITS LOCATION
===========================================================
Source: S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024), review 'Passage of Particles Through Matter', §34.2.3 ('Stopping power at intermediate energies'), chapter page 5 (the page footer reads '5  34. Passage of Particles Through Matter'). URL: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf.

Verbatim, immediately following Eq. (34.5):

  "Eq. (34.5) is valid in the region 0.1 . βγ . 1000 with an accuracy of a few percent. At βγ ∼ 0.1 the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron "speed," and at βγ ∼ 1000 radiative effects begin to be important (Sec. 34.6). Both limits are Z dependent."

(PDG typography uses '.' for '≲'; the sentence therefore reads 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000.)

For completeness, the equation the sentence governs is the Bethe equation for the mean mass stopping power of a moderately relativistic charged heavy particle (review's own wording: 'The mean rate of energy loss by moderately relativistic charged heavy particles is well described by the "Bethe equation"'):

  −dE/dx = K z² (Z/A) (1/β²) [ ½ ln( 2 m_e c² β²γ² W_max / I² ) − β² − δ(βγ)/2 ]      (34.5)

with the review's footnote stating that this is the mass stopping power in MeV g⁻¹ cm², and that the linear stopping power in MeV/cm is ρ·dE/dx (ρ in g/cm³).

===========================================================
2. ASK 1 — VERDICT: NO. THE STATED VALIDITY REGION DOES NOT SUPPORT THE USE.
===========================================================
βγ = 0.01 lies outside the stated region 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000, by a factor of 10 in βγ. The review's few-percent accuracy is stated over that interval and over nothing else. The analyst's proposed use is therefore not covered.

Three independent statements in the same chapter all point the same way, so the verdict does not rest on a single clause:

(a) The interval itself: 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000. Operating point 0.01. Ratio 0.1/0.01 = 10 in βγ (in β: 0.0995/0.0099995 = 9.95; in the 1/β² factor that dominates there: ≈ 99).

(b) The review's own explanation of the lower bound: 'At βγ ∼ 0.1 the projectile speed is comparable to atomic electron "speed"' — i.e. the lower bound marks the breakdown of the fast-projectile premise on which the equation rests, and it is placed at β ≈ 0.1, not β ≈ 0.01.

(c) The review's explicit low-energy warning, in the same chapter: 'The theory of energy loss by ionization and excitation as given by Bethe is based on a first-order Born approximation. It assumes free electrons, and should be valid when the projectile's speed is large compared to that of the atomic electrons. This presents a problem at low energies, where Wmax is less than the K shell binding energy.' This is precisely the regime βγ = 0.01 occupies (quantified in §4 below).

The accuracy qualifier and the validity interval are not separable. The phrase 'with an accuracy of a few percent' sits in the same sentence as 'valid in the region 0.1 . βγ . 1000', attached to Eq. (34.5) itself — not to a broader regime description elsewhere in the chapter. There is therefore no reading under which the few-percent claim survives outside the interval: the interval and the accuracy are one statement. (This resolves the third scoping question in the research notes: the qualifier belongs to Eq. (34.5), not to a separate regime discussion.)

One further scope point the analyst should not overlook: Eq. (34.5) is stated for 'moderately relativistic charged heavy particles'. A βγ = 0.01 electron is not within the stated scope of the equation at all, independently of the βγ bound.

===========================================================
3. ASK 2 — THE βγ REGION OVER WHICH THE ACCURACY IS STATED
===========================================================
Stated region: 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000, dimensionless (βγ ≡ p/Mc). Accuracy quoted: 'a few percent'. Location: §34.2.3, chapter page 5, prose immediately after Eq. (34.5) — prose, not a figure caption.

The bounds are approximate as written: the review uses '.' (≲) in the validity sentence and '∼0.1' / '∼1000' in the explanatory sentence, and it states 'Both limits are Z dependent.' The review does not quantify that Z dependence or give per-material bounds. The region should therefore be quoted as 0.1 ≲ βγ ≲ 1000 with the Z-dependence caveat, not as a hard-edged interval.

===========================================================
4. WHERE THE OPERATING POINT SITS — ARITHMETIC (derived here; not quoted from the review)
===========================================================
At βγ = 0.01: (βγ)² = 1.0000 × 10⁻⁴; γ = √(1 + (βγ)²) = 1.000050; β = (βγ)/γ = 0.0099995; γ − 1 = 4.9999 × 10⁻⁵.
Kinetic energy T = M c² (γ − 1), using CODATA masses (m_e c² = 0.510999 MeV; m_μ c² = 105.658 MeV; m_π± c² = 139.570 MeV; m_p c² = 938.272 MeV; m_K± c² = 493.677 MeV):

  particle   T at βγ = 0.01
  proton     46.91 keV
  charged pion 6.978 keV
  charged kaon 24.68 keV
  muon       5.283 keV
  electron   25.55 eV   (outside the stated scope of Eq. (34.5); listed only to show the scale)

Maximum energy transfer, W_max = 2 m_e c² (βγ)² / [1 + 2γ m_e/M + (m_e/M)²], evaluated at βγ = 0.01:
  proton: W_max = 1.0209 × 10⁻⁴ MeV = 102.1 eV
  muon:   W_max = 1.0122 × 10⁻⁴ MeV = 101.2 eV
(At this βγ the denominator is ≈ 1 for any M ≥ m_μ, so W_max ≈ 2 m_e c² (βγ)² ≈ 102 eV, essentially mass independent.)

Consequence, tied directly to the review's own caveat (c) above: W_max ≈ 1.0 × 10² eV is of the order of, or below, the K-shell binding energies of all but the lightest elements (H 13.6 eV, C ≈ 284 eV; standard NIST x-ray values, not from the fetched PDG text — reviewer to confirm if used quantitatively). The review's stated low-energy concern therefore applies at the analyst's operating point, not merely in principle.

Consistency check performed on this draft: 0.01 < 0.1 (verdict No), the region quoted is 0.1–1000 (matches the verdict), the derived kinetic energies are all far below any regime where the review claims few-percent accuracy, and W_max < typical K-shell energies (matches caveat c). No number in this draft contradicts a bound stated elsewhere in it.

===========================================================
5. CAVEATS AND TEXTUAL UNCERTAINTIES (stated so the reviewer can weigh them)
===========================================================
(i) 'A few percent' is never quantified numerically in the sentence or its neighbourhood. The chapter does contain quantified deviations — 'The rms deviation is 2.2% for the solids and 4.0% for the gases' — but that passage appears in the discussion of Sternheimer's density-effect parameterisation (the adjacent text reads 'The density effect correction is usually computed using Sternheimer's parameterization [17]:'), i.e. it is a fit residual for δ(βγ), not the tolerance on Eq. (34.5). Do not substitute 2.2%/4.0% for 'a few percent'.
(ii) The direction of the stated Z dependence is not given in the review. It cannot rescue the analyst's use: the lower bound is set by the breakdown of the fast-projectile/free-electron premise at β ≈ atomic-electron speed, so a material-dependent shift of that bound would move it in the wrong direction (higher, for tightly bound electrons), and in any case no material-specific exception reaching βγ = 0.01 is stated anywhere in the chapter.
(iii) The bounds are stated with '.' (≲) and '∼', so they are soft. Even the most generous reading of that softness (tens of percent) does not reach 0.01, a decade lower.
(iv) The chapter also contains a page-break fragment ending the preceding section: 'at very low energies [8]. dE/dx in the radiative region is not simply a function of β.' It is a truncated sentence and is cited here only as corroboration that the review acknowledges low-energy departures; it is not load-bearing for the verdict.
(v) This determination says nothing about the numerical value of dE/dx at βγ = 0.01. An illustrative evaluation of the Bethe bracket at βγ = 0.01 for carbon (inputs K = 0.307075 MeV g⁻¹ cm², Z/A = 6/12.011, I = 78.0 eV — none of which were present in the fetched passages; reviewer must confirm against PDG Table 34.1) gives a bracket ≈ 0.27 and a mass stopping power of order 4 × 10² MeV g⁻¹ cm². This is quoted ONLY to show that the logarithm has collapsed to O(0.3) there, so the result is dominated by the 1/β² factor and is acutely sensitive to I and to shell corrections — exactly the regime where the review claims nothing. It is not a validated stopping power and must not be used as one.

===========================================================
6. EDITION CHECK (sample size N = 2 copies)
===========================================================
The governing sentence was checked in two independently fetched copies and is identical in both:
  (a) https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf (page footer '25th March, 2025'), sha256 1b328278e835…;
  (b) the copy hosted under https://pdg.lbl.gov/2026/download/rpp-2025/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf (page footer '31st May, 2024'), sha256 3ead731273e0….
Both carry the same chapter numbering (Eq. 34.5, §34.2.3) and the same validity sentence word for word. The verdict is therefore insensitive to which of these two copies is treated as authoritative; the differing page footers are a version artefact, not a content difference. Citation for publication: S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024).

===========================================================
7. WHAT THE ANALYST MAY AND MAY NOT CLAIM
===========================================================

The defining sentence does three distinct things, and each matters for the worksheet:

1. **It binds the symbol.** The symbol used is exactly `Rj` — the same symbol the worksheet uses.
2. **It names the quantity.** "Jovian **model** radius". It is not worded as a mean radius, an equatorial radius, a polar radius, or a volumetric radius. This is the only retrieved source that attaches the symbol Rj to a *model* radius.

N = 1 collision on average, for a beta ~ 1 particle, with Te > 10 keV, along 90 cm of argon gas.

=== 3. INDEPENDENT RECOMPUTATION (verification that 'one' is not a typo or a transcription slip) ===

Integrating Eq. (34.9) above Tcut with F(T) ~ 1 (valid for T << Wmax):

  N(>Tcut) = (1/2) K z^2 (Z/A) beta^-2 [ 1/Tcut - 1/Wmax ] * rho * L

  K        = 0.307075 MeV mol^-1 cm^2   (PDG Eq. 34.5 constant; Table 34.1)
  z        = 1                          (projectile, z=1 assumed throughout the review)
  Z/A      = 18 / 39.948 = 0.45059 mol g^-1  (argon; PDG AtomicNuclearProperties)
  beta     = 1                          (as specified in the review's example)

  rho(Ar)  = 1.7837e-3 g cm^-3 at 0 degC/101.325 kPa (STP); 1.6623e-3 g cm^-3 at 20 degC
